difficultyRationale: A pagination cost that's invisible in the code and only shows up as an extra query in the SQL log, which is exactly the kind of thing a senior candidate should flag before it becomes a production surprise.
prompt: A repository method `Page<Order> findByStatus(String status, Pageable pageable)` backs a paginated API endpoint. Besides returning the requested page of content, what else does Spring Data JPA do by default to produce that `Page<Order>`?
explanation: A `Page<T>` carries `totalElements` and `totalPages` in addition to the page's content, and Spring Data computes those by issuing a second query — a `COUNT` query built from the same conditions as the content query — rather than deriving the total from the page it just fetched. So a single call to a `Page`-returning method executes at least two SQL statements, which matters when the underlying table is large and the COUNT itself becomes expensive.

options.text: A Page object never carries a total count unless the caller explicitly calls repository.count() afterward as a separate, manually written statement; by itself, findByStatus(..., pageable) issues only the one paged SELECT and leaves totalElements at zero.
options.explanation: Populating totalElements/totalPages is exactly what distinguishes Page from the lighter Slice return type, and Spring Data issues the COUNT query itself, automatically, as part of fulfilling a Page-returning method — the caller doesn't have to request it separately.

options.text: Spring Data computes the total element count purely in the JVM: it loads every row matching the condition into memory once, counts the resulting list's size, and then discards everything outside the requested page before returning the Page object.
options.explanation: That would defeat the entire purpose of pagination (avoiding loading the full result set) and isn't how it works; Spring Data counts at the database with a COUNT query instead of ever materializing the full result set in application memory.

options.text: Spring Data issues a separate COUNT query derived from the same WHERE conditions to populate totalElements and totalPages on the returned Page, so a single findByStatus(..., pageable) call executes at least two SQL statements, not one.
options.explanation: Correct. The content query and the count query are two separate round trips to the database, and the count query can be the more expensive of the two on a large, unindexed table.

options.text: Pageable queries always execute as a single SQL statement that uses a database-specific window function to compute the page content and the total count together, regardless of which database is configured for the application.
options.explanation: Spring Data's standard Page support issues two separate, portable statements (a content query and a COUNT query) rather than relying on a database-specific window-function trick that would tie pagination to one vendor's SQL dialect.

references.title: Spring Data JPA Reference Documentation — Query Methods ("A Page knows about the total number of elements and pages available. It does so by the infrastructure triggering a count query to calculate the overall number.")
